title: What Bad Leadership Can Teach Good Leaders
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Admired Leadership argues that many of the best leaders credit bad role models with shaping their approach. Those who endure poor leadership often resolve to do the opposite once they have influence, inventing a style that produces the reverse of what they felt. The example is a leader who suffered under a supervisor who hoarded information and punished bad news, and who later made transparency a signature. The piece claims pain is a remarkably good teacher because it shows exactly where damage happens and so what the repair must be. Good role models make leadership look effortless and therefore hard to copy, while a bad leader leaves every flaw exposed and memorable. The closing advice for anyone under a terrible leader is that every bad leader leaves a blueprint that the best leaders build in reverse.
points: Leaders who endured dysfunctional bosses often build their style as the deliberate opposite of what they experienced.
A leader who suffered under information hoarding and punished bad news may later make transparency, early numbers and treating mistakes as data their signature.
Skilled leaders make the craft look effortless, so good examples are hard to copy, whereas bad leaders expose every flaw vividly.
Remembering how specific moments and behaviors felt gives developing leaders concrete ingredients for something better.
If you work under a terrible leader now, treat their behavior as a blueprint of what not to do.
quotes: In many cases, leaders who endure an awful leader dedicate themselves to doing the opposite once they gain influence. They invent a leadership style that produces the opposite effect on others from what they experienced.
They didn’t learn this from a mentor who modeled it well. They learned it by feeling, day after day, what its absence cost.
Pain is a remarkably good teacher. It shows exactly where the damage happens, and so exactly what the repair must be.
Good role models, by contrast, can make leadership look effortless, and effortless is hard to copy. When a skilled leader handles a tense moment with grace, the craft behind it is often invisible.

For those who go on to become exceptional leaders, suffering under poor leadership can make them unusually attentive to small moments and specific behaviors. By remembering how those moments and behaviors felt, they gain the core ingredients to develop something different and better.
The worst leaders rarely mean to teach anything. But for those paying attention, they may end up teaching exactly what not to do, and that lesson may be the most valuable of all.
If you work under a terrible leader right now, remember this: Every bad leader leaves a blueprint. The best leaders simply build it in reverse.
